epithet: Hawari al-Nabi (The Disciple of the Prophet)
role: One of the Ten Promised Paradise
Nephew and disciple of the Prophet ﷺ
summary: Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (RA) was one of the Ten Companions promised Paradise and the Prophet's ﷺ own nephew through his mother Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib. Among the earliest converts, he is said to have been the first to draw a sword in the cause of Islam. Known as Hawari al-Nabi, he fought in every major battle and was distinguished for his unmatched personal courage on the battlefield.
biography:
Zubayr ibn al-Awwam al-Asadi al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 594 CE. His father was al-Awwam ibn Khuwaylid and his mother was Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib, making him the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ cousin — his maternal aunt's son. His father-in-law was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA), whose daughter Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) he married, a pairing that linked two of the most distinguished Companions.

Zubayr accepted Islam at a very young age, traditionally said to be around twelve years old, making him among the earliest converts. Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra records that when news reached Makkah that the Prophet ﷺ had been captured — a false rumor — Zubayr immediately drew his sword and ran to find him, prepared to fight whoever held him. This is said to be the first time a sword was drawn in defense of the Prophet ﷺ, earning him lifelong distinction. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the title Hawari al-Nabi — 'my disciple,' as in one wholly devoted to him — a title the Prophet ﷺ himself stated: 'Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is Zubayr ibn al-Awwam.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Jihad; Sahih Muslim, Kitab Fada'il al-Sahaba).

He endured early persecution in Makkah; classical sources record that his uncle Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid wrapped him in a mat and subjected him to smoke to force apostasy, but he refused. He participated in the migration to Abyssinia with some early Muslims but returned and later made the Hijrah to Madinah.

In every major battle of the Prophet's era, Zubayr fought with distinction. At Badr (2 AH), he was in the vanguard. At Uhud (3 AH), when many scattered after the archers abandoned their post, Zubayr remained near the Prophet ﷺ alongside Talha ibn Ubayd Allah. At al-Khandaq (5 AH), the Prophet ﷺ sent him on a reconnaissance mission against the Banu Qurayza. At Khaybar, during the siege and battles with the Jewish fortresses (7 AH), he fought in the front. He participated in the conquest of Makkah (8 AH) and the Battle of Hunayn, and was present at the expedition to Tabuk.

After the Prophet's ﷺ death, Zubayr continued serving the Muslim community in the great conquests under Abu Bakr and Umar (RA). He fought in Egypt during the Islamic conquest, and al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' notes his role in the siege and fall of Alexandria. He was named one of the six members of Umar's shura council to choose the next caliph — reserved for those the Prophet ﷺ had promised Paradise.

Like Talha (RA), Zubayr's life concluded in the fitna period. He traveled with Talha and Aisha (RA) to Basra, calling for justice for the murdered caliph Uthman ibn Affan (RA). The resulting Battle of the Camel in 36 AH (656 CE) is one of the most sorrowfully examined events in Islamic history. Classical Sunni scholars hold that all the main participants — including Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA), Talha (RA), Zubayr (RA), and Aisha (RA) — were sincere believers acting on their best ijtihad. Zubayr withdrew from the fighting before it reached its most intense stage, apparently moved by a reminder from Ali (RA) of a statement the Prophet ﷺ had made. He was killed while withdrawing by Ibn Jurmuz, an act that Ali (RA) reportedly condemned as the murder of one who had withdrawn from battle. He was martyred near Wadi al-Siba' outside Basra.

Zubayr left considerable wealth and estates but also debts he had taken on to help companions in need; his son Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (RA) organized the repayment of those debts after his death, a story preserved in detail by al-Bukhari in his Tarikh. He narrated approximately 38 hadith in the major collections.
